en: Instruction on Reality.
For the sake of purifying the meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam*, the Guru spoke these words to the disciple:
"In this sentence *tattvamasi*, analyze the meaning of the word *tvam*. (1)
You are not the body, because it is an object of perception, because it possesses genus and other such qualities, and likewise because it is composed of the elements, impure, and impermanent. (2)

You are invisible, devoid of form, and though devoid of birth, you are not composed of the elements; you are pure and eternal, whose nature is vision, for as a pot cannot become vision, so [the body] cannot become you. || 3 ||
Your scriptural statement that you are the instrument of these senses is not [correct];
for you are their impeller, distinct from them. An agent cannot be an instrument. || 4 ||
It is not that you are of the same nature as these [elements]; hear why you are distinct from them:
nor are you of the nature of a single sense-organ, because the notion of "I" is present everywhere. (5)
You are neither their collection nor any one of them;
for even upon the destruction of those [elements], the cognition of a self persists, which would not be the case otherwise.
Even individually, the self is not present in them; hear the reasoning for this:
this body has various owners and would perish if it were to rely on conflicting opinions. (7)
The [notion of] a manifold self is not [tenable], because their objects would be contradictory;
however, if there were unity of ownership, there would be a systematic arrangement, as in the case of a single king's domain. (8)
Neither is it the mind nor the vital breath, because both of these are insentient;
furthermore, from the experience of their distinctness, as in the thought, "My consciousness has gone elsewhere. (9)
Thinking "this life-force of mine is afflicted by hunger and thirst," one perceives them as distinct;
thus, the witness is separate from those two, just as the observer of a jar is distinct from the jar itself.
O twice-born one, that which is dissolved in sleep and pervades the entire body upon awakening, and which is connected by the shadow of consciousness—that is not the intellect (buddhi). || 11 ||
The intellect possesses various forms; it is dissolved in sleep and exceedingly restless.
Since you are the vision of a single form, you are its distinct illuminator.
Even in deep sleep, when the body and other such factors are absent, you remain the witness of them; because your nature is self-experience, there is no other illuminator for you.
Those people who, by means of a means of knowledge, desire to understand that very awareness which makes the means of knowledge known,
are like those who wish to burn fire with fuel.
The Self experiences the universe, yet It is not experienced by it;
the Self illumines the universe, yet It is not illumined by it. 15.
Suchness and thatness—this is not something hidden, for it is existence itself.
Therefore, you are the Brahman; you are not of the nature of the visible body and so forth, but are the all-seeing witness. 16.
Everything that appears as "this-ness" is negated;
the ineffable reality is not "this," for it is not an object of knowledge, being self-luminous. || 17 ||
Truth, knowledge, and infinity are said to be the defining characteristics of Brahman;
indeed, because you possess truth, the nature of knowledge, and infinity, you alone are that.

When the limiting adjuncts such as the body exist, there is the individual soul (jīva) and its controller, the Lord (īśvara), due to the adjunct of [His] power; when both are sublated, He is self-luminous. || 19 ||

That which is not dependent upon any other means of knowledge, yet itself depends on no other means of knowledge—that Vedic statement is held to be the authoritative means for the realization of the Brahman-Ātman. (20)
Therefore, we shall now fully set forth the reasoning by which the Vedic statement "That thou art" and others are established as authoritative for the Brahmin. (21)
For when the referent of the term "thou" has been purified, the Great Sayings such as "That thou art" can be contemplated;
it is not possible otherwise. Therefore, purification was performed at the outset.

That which superimposes falsely upon its own self attributes such as the body and the senses, and possesses the conceit of agency and so forth—that is the denoted meaning of the word "thou" (tvaṃpada). || 23 ||

That witness of the body, senses, and so forth, who shines forth as distinct from them, and who, by virtue of being self-luminous consciousness, is the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpada). || 24 ||

That which is to be known through the Vedānta texts, which transcends the universe, which is imperishable and non-dual, pure, and self-evident—that is the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) of the word "That" (tat). || 25 ||
For grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) belongs to two words, just as it does to the two terms "that" (tat) and "thou" (tvam).
Through this, the identity of Brahman and the individual self is established by the Vedāntas. (26)
When two words have different grounds for their application yet both function with respect to a single object, there is likewise a unity between those two words ending in case-terminations. (27)
Grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is asserted by the followers of that tradition;
likewise, there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two word-meanings themselves. (28)
A relationship between two things occurs like that of "this is that" or "that is this";
[in this case], there is inwardness (pratyaktva) along with duality, as well as remoteness (parokṣatva) and fullness (pūrṇatā). 29.
Since they would be mutually contradictory, there arises [the need for] indication (lakṣaṇā).
The relationship between the object to be defined and its definition is that between the word-meaning and the inner self. || 30 ||

And when the primary meaning cannot be accepted because it is contradicted by another means of knowledge, the application [of a word] to that which is invariably connected with the primary meaning is called indication (lakṣaṇā). // 31 //
The indication (lakṣaṇā) is to be known as threefold: the abandoning, the non-abandoning, and likewise that which consists of both; among these, the first is simply not possible.
That function which, having abandoned the entire literal meaning, operates upon that which is associated with it—
as in "A hamlet on the Ganges"— is indeed *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own sense) indication.

In the present context, the abandonment of a portion of the literal meaning is desired; however, the *jahatsvārthā* [type of indication] cannot possibly occur here, as it would contradict established tradition. (34)
That function which, without abandoning the expressed meaning, conveys another meaning is called *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning), as in the example: "This red one runs. (35)
That [literal meaning] is also not possible here, due to extreme contradiction;
for in the present case, the abandonment of the contradictory element is observed. (36)

That which causes one to understand a single part [of the primary meaning] by abandoning another part of the expressed meaning is to be known as the third type, partial indication (bhāgalakṣaṇā). || 37 ||
Thus this Brahmin instructs these words from the beginning, characterized by that time and likewise joined with this time. (38)
Therefore, having set aside those contradictory properties such as "belonging to that specific time" and so forth, the sentence is said to convey the Brahmin's body just as it is. (39)

In the same way, listen to what is stated regarding the scriptural text "That thou art" (tattvamasi): one must discard from the word *tvam* the attributes of the individual soul, such as inwardness (*pratyaktva*) and the like. 40.
Having set aside omniscience, non-perceptibility, and so forth, that word "Tataḥ" respectfully indicates the pure, immutable, and non-dual reality. (41)
"O Tattvamasi, the identity of the two words 'That' and 'Thou' alone is sufficient;
through such an awakening to oneness, one should bring perfect knowledge to firmness by means of reasoning. (42)
He who possesses the realization "I am Brahman" crosses over sorrow;
likewise, through the Great Sayings (Mahāvākyas), the Self, though ever-luminous, [is realized as] oneness. 43.
Even if the reality is understood by following the sequence of what precedes and follows, it still cannot be realized at all without the compassion of the venerable Guru. 44.
In this world, for those who are deluded yet consider themselves wise,
knowledge manifests of its own accord once the internal organ has been purified, so that they may perceive it directly.
"Therefore, it is not right to ask what would be gained by a teacher through Vedic statements;
for the Śruti has declared: 'A man who possesses a teacher truly knows. (46)
In this beginningless saṃsāra, the Guru alone is indeed the awakener;
therefore, having realized the identity of the Brahman and the Self, one should perceive the visible world as non-existent. 47.
One should always abide in non-dual Brahman through the nature of the innermost Self;
through the direct perception of that, the non-dual Brahman, which is a mass of consciousness, is fully realized. 48.
That alone is to be established here by the Vedantas, and not a duality consisting of the insentient;
namely, the non-dual consciousness whose nature is bliss, and not that which is of the nature of suffering, unreal, and insentient. 49.
That non-duality has been correctly determined by the Vedāntas through the method of reasoning according to reality;
know that non-duality alone is true, while duality is always unreal. 50.
How could that which is impure exist within the pure? Therefore, the visible world is composed of illusion;
just as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is false, so too is the universe within the Supreme Self.
Existence does not arise from itself, nor does existence belong to that which is non-existent;
because it is subject to sublation, duality is neither real, yet it is not unreal either, since it appears to direct perception. (52)
Because existence and non-existence are contradictory, that [cause] is therefore truly indescribable;
it was previously one alone, and having created this world, it subsequently [became manifold]. (53)
Having entered in the form of the individual soul (jīva), you are that very same Supreme Self;
you are indeed Existence-Consciousness-Bliss, yet you have forgotten your supreme nature as the Self.
Through awakening, that very Self has attained the state of being the individual soul;
it is non-dual bliss, pure consciousness alone, and having become purified, it has attained sovereign dominion.
Those attributes such as agency and the like which previously resided in you, the supreme Brahman, having now investigated them, what is their true nature in reality? (56)
In this very context, hear a marvelous account spoken by the Vedas:
there was a certain man from the land of Gandhāra, adorned with great jewels. (57)
Once, while sleeping heedlessly in his own house and courtyard at night,
a thief arrived, lured by the sight of his ornaments.
Bound by thieves and led to another country through a dense forest, he was stripped of his ornaments and had his eyes, hands, and feet tied. (59)
He was cast into a forest exceedingly thick with kusha grass, thorns, and scorpions,
crowded with serpents, tigers, and other beasts, and dense with trees.
Afflicted by fear in the great forest due to predatory beasts and other wicked creatures.
By means of stones, thorns, darbha grass, and other such things that are adverse to the body; || 61 ||
While being rolled about, his limbs shattered and rendered powerless,
he is tormented by hunger, thirst, heat, wind, fire, and other such extreme afflictions.
In that very place, he saw someone who had been released from bondage and was standing there alone, crying out with a mind full of great suffering as he reached his destination. || 63 ||
Likewise, by the groups of enemies such as passion and the rest who bestow suffering, and by the thieves such as the conceit of a body and so forth who steal the wealth of one's own bliss. (64)
Intoxicated by the bliss of the intellect and overcome by the sleep of your own ignorance, you are firmly bound by fetters such as the fever of craving for worldly enjoyments. 65.
Having been forcibly displaced from your true nature, which is non-dual bliss, you have been led far away by great deceivers into bodies within the forest lands of saṃsāra. 66.
In all the causes of suffering—the triad beginning with the body—and in various wombs fashioned by the latent impressions of karma, [one wanders]. (67)
You have been made to enter, you have been created, and you have been bound by the vision of your own bliss;
yet, from beginningless time, you have always experienced suffering. (68)
The succession of birth, death, old age, defects, hell, and so forth.
Constantly dejected, he experienced extreme sorrow. || 69 ||

Although the bondage born of ignorance had ceased and the giver of suffering was gone, and though he had attained the bliss of his own true nature, he did not find the means to [communicate] that Truth. (70)
Just as one from the land of Gandhāra, having long been bound by the fetters of sight and so forth due to fate, was released by certain compassionate travelers who encountered him. (71)
Instructed by those established in well-being, that wise man, firm in his resolve,
should go from village to village, being intelligent and intent upon the path.
Having gone to the land of Gāndhāra and reached his own home as before, he was embraced by his kinsmen and remained there in happiness. || 73 ||
You too, having wandered through many such births that bring suffering, have by chance been born with faith in the auspicious path and have performed virtuous deeds. (74)
Devoted to the conduct of the castes and stages of life, he had attained the great rise of merit;
through the grace of the Lord, he obtained the most excellent teacher, a knower of the Veda.
Having duly performed renunciation, being wise and endowed with discernment and other virtues, he has today attained the supreme instruction regarding Brahman through the practice of dispassion. (76)
The wise and intelligent person, investigating reality through reasoning and endowed with profound meditation, has indeed attained the supreme state— you have reached it.
Therefore, O wise one, the knowledge of the Brahman-self has been taught to you by me, your teacher, according to the rule; apply yourself to it with perfect diligence.
Having become one whose bonds are liberated and whose doubts regarding the nature of non-duality are severed,
wander at your ease, free from attachment and devoid of longing.

In reality, you are free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) and eternally liberated by your very nature; for you, there is neither bondage nor liberation, since those two are merely imagined within you. 80.
There is no cessation and no arising; there is no one bound and no practitioner; there is no seeker of liberation and no one liberated—this is the ultimate reality. 81.
Having thus reflected with your own intellect upon this essence of the Vedantic conclusions,
you should meditate deeply upon the Supreme, whose nature is one's own bliss.
Having personally realized the indivisible, non-dual, imperishable Brahman, you are liberated even while living; rest in peace, having attained tranquility. 83.
The Vedāntas are to be investigated, and the Guru is always to be revered;
for men, the word of the Gurus is wholesome, as is their sight and their service. 84.
The Guru is the very heart and is himself directly to be served and saluted by those seeking liberation;
he must certainly not be provoked by one who is grateful and discerning. 85.
For as long as you live, you must revere Vedānta as your Guru and Lord—through mind, deed, and speech; this indeed is the certainty of the Śruti. 86.
One should always maintain non-duality regarding all things, but never non-duality regarding ritual actions;
there may be non-duality throughout the three worlds, but never non-duality with one's teacher.

Thus ends the *Tattvopadeśa*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*).
